title: Kunti meets Karna by the river
hookLine: Karna is at his prayers on the riverbank, facing the sun, and the woman waiting in his shadow is his mother.
carry: dana: give what you can, expecting nothing back
tomorrow: why would a blind king refuse to see?

cards: On the bank of the Ganga, a man stands facing east with his hands raised, reciting his prayers. The sun climbs until it burns his back, and he doesn't move.
Behind him, a woman has come quietly and stands in the shade of his own upper cloth, waiting until he's finished. It's Kunti, and the man is Karna. Yesterday, Krishna asked Karna to change sides.
Today, his mother comes to ask the same thing, in person.

teach.h: YOU ARE MINE, AND THE SUN'S
teach.b: Karna finishes, turns, and greets her by naming himself: I am Karna, son of Radha and Adhiratha. What can I do for you? Kunti tells him the truth.
You are not a charioteer's son. You are mine, and the Sun's. Come to your brothers.
In the text, a voice even speaks from the sun to confirm her words. But his answer is hard to hear. You cast me away when I was born.
You never gave me a mother's care. Now, on the eve of war, you come to me for the sake of your other sons.
And then, after the hardest words, Karna gives her something. He won't join the Pandavas, but he makes a promise.
In the battle he will not kill four of her sons, Yudhishthira, Bhima, Nakula and Sahadeva, even when he has them at his mercy. Only Arjuna will he fight to the end.

teach.h: FIVE SONS, AND THE GIVEN ARMOR
teach.b: Either way, he says, you will still have five sons: with Arjuna, or with me. Kunti embraces him, and they part. That's Karna.
Earlier in the epic, Indra came to him disguised as a brahmin and asked for the armor he was born with, and Karna cut it from his own body and gave it.
Many Hindus still remember him as Daanveer Karna, Karna the hero of giving.
Dana, giving, is one of the oldest duties in Hindu life, and the Gita calls the purest gift the one given because giving is right, expecting nothing back.
Karna can't give his mother what she came for. So he gives what he can, and it may cost him his life.

how: Kunti's meeting with Karna on the Ganga bank is read in the Udyoga book of the Mahabharata and retold in story, poetry and performance, where Karna is often remembered as Daanveer Karna, the great giver.

games.q: you're Karna. your birth mother asks you to join your brothers on the eve of war. you've already refused Krishna. what do you do?
o: refuse her completely and send her away.
refuse, but promise to spare four of her sons.
games.why: Karna stays with Duryodhana, but still gives: he will fight only Arjuna to the end, so she will still have five sons. dana: he gives what he can.

practice: Think of someone who asked for something you can't fully give. Breathing in, admit what you can't give; breathing out, choose one thing you can. Give it today as dana: quietly, expecting nothing back.
If you pray, offer it to God as you give; if not, simply let it go.

wordCard.voice: Udyoga. The book of getting ready. Our days with it end here, on choices made by a river, before the armies take the field.

orig.note: Karna, Kunti's first son, raised by the charioteer Adhiratha and his wife Radha.

carryVoice: Your line: dana: give what you can, expecting nothing back. Karna spared four sons, so she will still have five. Tomorrow: why would a blind king refuse to see?
